source.title: Specialization, Diversity, and Scaling in Child-Scale Language Models
source.authors: Steven Y. Feng; Michael C. Frank

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present. Some figure and table layout is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests child-scale held-out-loss curves and finds that its pre-specified standard power-law fit checks fail for every core curve. It also reports sensitivity of scaling comparisons to training recipe, while explicitly limiting its conclusions to the tested setting.
record.gate_note: The paper cites large-scale scaling-law work as background but does not test compute-optimal allocation. It varies training-data size, not compute at fixed budget. Its cross-child specialization, synthetic-distribution, and diversity findings are recorded only where they bear on the claim's subject; the fixed-budget diversity results are not themselves tests of a power-law scaling curve.
record.test_reason: The study fits a standard power law to held-out loss against training-data size over 25k–3.2M words, for two GPT-2 sizes on two corpora. None of the four core curves passes the authors' pre-specified fit checks, and a log-linear alternative is preferred by AICc. This is a new, child-scale setting with a result on V1 and V7, so T3. It could also be read as T5, but the authors limit the finding to this setting and fitting procedure. The paper does not test parameter or compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, shape, other modalities, or large-scale extrapolation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct but incomplete. The authors' main conclusion is that small-data LM performance depends on which environments the input comes from and how well it matches the evaluation data, not only on quantity. Models specialize strongly and lastingly to individual children's environments, largely through lexical and distributional effects. Diversity at a fixed budget helps pooled prediction more clearly than grammar benchmarks. On scaling, the learning curves improve with data, but a single standard power law fails their pre-specified checks in this low-data range. They state this explicitly as a limited result, not a rejection of power-law scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies child-scale text data and evaluates fixed-recipe learning curves, with validation-selected checkpoints and a separate bounded recipe-sensitivity grid. It does not reproduce the large-scale parameter/token/compute sweeps or compute-optimal allocation procedure of the cited original work.
record.method_sensitivity: Training recipe changes the GPT-2/KN-5 vocabulary-aligned crossover in three of four comparisons. The paper also states that power-law adequacy depends on its specified fitting procedure and does not exclude relationships under other setups or fitting procedures.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 100k-word budget, adding contributing children improves pooled held-out BPW (slope −0.124 per ln k). Zorro shows no clear trend (p=.28).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed small-data budget, training-data diversity and distributional match affect held-out loss more than grammatical-benchmark performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Tuning learning rate, dropout, weight decay and training length moves the data size at which GPT-2 overtakes a 5-gram model one tested size earlier in 3 of 4 comparisons. The original recipe was never selected.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At low data, which architecture or baseline wins on held-out loss depends on the training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched data sizes, natural and synthetic sources, and mixed-age versus age-2 sources, give different Zorro and WordSim profiles. The sign of some differences changes with data size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The composition of training data, not only its quantity, shapes downstream benchmark profiles at small scale.

record.problems: The scaling range is child-scale and the comparisons match sampled word occurrences rather than optimization steps or compute; the authors explicitly do not call them compute-optimal curves. There are only three corpus draws in the replicated scaling series, and the authors note limits to bootstrap precision and no correction for multiple comparisons. The power-law conclusion is specific to stringent pre-specified fit checks and does not rule out other fitting procedures or setups.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were omitted for the 60-row cap. Other reported experiments on specialization, persistence, word acquisition, and child-specific vocabulary do not test the listed scaling versions.

untested.parts: Scaling in parameters and compute. Data scaling beyond about 2 orders of magnitude (25k–3.2M words). Data scaling under tuned or compute-matched training.
All. Leave-one-size-out checks are within the range, not extrapolation orders of magnitude larger.
All. No fixed-compute sweep; the authors say the curves are not compute-optimal.
All. Only two model sizes; no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
All. Text only; no other modalities, repeated-data laws, fine-tuning or transfer.
Raw benchmark-versus-size trends appear only in Figures 4 and 10, with no numbers in the text. The relation between benchmark scores and pretraining loss is not analysed.
Exponents across parameter-counting conventions, data sources or fitting methods. Effects on the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Per-curve fit results for the other three core curves (fitted β, which of criteria A1–A5 failed, AICc values). Also leave-one-size-out accuracy: only 0–2 of 8 sizes predicted within 2 SD in representative cases.

Raw Zorro and WordSim accuracy versus training size for each corpus and model, which would bear on V6. The text gives only the 25k point (59.44% vs 48.41% at random initialization) and no trend numbers.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling is a secondary diagnostic in this paper; its stated goal is to characterize child-scale scaling, not to test scaling laws. I downgraded V1 from 'challenges' to 'limits_scope' for four reasons: loss does decrease, the range is only about 2 orders of magnitude, the fixed recipe is shown to be suboptimal, and the authors disclaim generality. I removed the V6 links because all V6 rows measure source or composition differences, not improvement with scale. I removed the V7 links from the recipe and crossover rows because they do not measure exponents or splits. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Tests training-data size in the child-scale regime only; does not test parameter-count or compute scaling, or several orders of magnitude at large-model scales.
The paper includes leave-one-data-size-out diagnostics, but does not test whether laws fitted on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested. The paper explicitly says its comparisons are not compute-optimal learning curves.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at a fixed parameter count.
The study uses text data and does not test other modalities, repeated-data scaling, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Evaluates Zorro, BLiMP, and WordSim across selected data sizes and sources, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss or extrapolates to larger scales.

Tests recipe sensitivity and standard power-law fit adequacy in this child-scale setting; does not compare fitted exponents across parameter-counting conventions or compute-optimal splits across broader setups.

rows.subject: GPT-2 micro
rows.operation_detail: Fit held-out loss against training-data size using L(N) = L∞ + AN^−β.
rows.measure: Adequacy of standard power-law fit under five pre-specified criteria
rows.value: No core fit passed all criteria. The reported BabyView micro example had weighted R² = 0.965; AICc was 71.9 for the power law and 58.5 for the log-linear alternative.
rows.note: The authors say the standard power law did not adequately summarize the observed curves under this test, while cautioning that this is not a general rejection of power-law scaling.
rows.check: State 'absent' is too strong for V1. Loss does fall with data (text: curves 'improve overall with data'), but the power-law form fails the criteria: weighted R² 0.965 is below the 0.98 threshold, and AICc is 71.9 for the power law versus 58.5 for log-linear. So V1 is partial. For V7 (curves bend away from a single power law), this row counts as observed.

relationships.condition: Child-scale data scaling (25k–3.2M words), GPT-2 micro and small, BabyView and age-2 TinyDialogues, fixed 20-epoch recipe, validation-selected checkpoint
relationships.reason: Loss falls with data, but a single power law failed the pre-specified checks on all four core curves. Log-linear is preferred by AICc (71.9 vs 58.5) and R² is 0.965 (R1–R4). The authors say this is not a general rejection of power laws, and the setting is about 2 orders of magnitude with a non-optimal recipe, so the result qualifies V1 rather than challenging it.

tranche.reason: The study explicitly tests power-law adequacy and finds that none of four core curves passes its criteria, qualifying V1 and supporting V7. T5 captures this qualification more specifically than the new-setting designation.
